sections.markdown:
## C — Tennessee safety belt and child restraint laws: who must buckle up, car seat and booster rules, driver and parent responsibility, how belts protect, correct belt fit, air bag safety, pickup bed limits and leaving children unattended
Knowledge domain: the Tennessee rules on who must wear a safety belt and when, which child restraint each age and size of child needs, who is responsible and what it costs to break the rules, how belts and air bags protect occupants and how to wear them, where children should sit, the pickup bed limits, and the offense of leaving a young child alone in a vehicle.

FACT_ID: sec06-F01 | anchor: A01
Tennessee law requires safety belts, child safety seats and booster seats, and an officer may stop and ticket a driver for a belt or child restraint violation alone. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F02 | anchor: A01
Every driver and every front-seat passenger must wear a safety belt whenever the vehicle is moving. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F03 | anchor: A01
Back-seat passengers under 17 years old must also wear safety belts. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F04 | anchor: A01
When the driver holds a learner permit or an intermediate license, back-seat passengers aged four to 17 must be belted. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F05 | anchor: A01
Tennessee was the first state to pass a Child Passenger Protection Law requiring children to ride in car seats and booster seats. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F06 | anchor: A01
A child under one year old, or any child under 20 pounds, must ride in a rear-facing car seat. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F07 | anchor: A01
A child aged one through three who weighs more than 20 pounds must ride in a forward-facing car seat. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F08 | anchor: A01
A child aged four through eight who is shorter than four feet, nine inches must ride in a belt-positioning booster seat while wearing a seat belt. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F09 | anchor: A01
A child in a booster seat must ride in the back seat whenever the vehicle has one, and every car seat and booster must meet federal safety standards and be used as its maker and the vehicle maker direct. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F10 | anchor: A01
The driver is responsible for restraining every child under 16 and can be charged and fined $50 when such a child is not properly restrained. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F11 | anchor: A01
When a child's parent or legal guardian is in the car but not driving, that parent or guardian is responsible for the child's restraint and can be fined. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F12 | anchor: A01
Failing to use a required car seat or booster seat for a child under nine, or one shorter than four feet, nine inches, can be charged as a Class C misdemeanor, with a required class on safely transporting children plus fees and fines. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F13 | anchor: A01
A child may ride in a medically prescribed modified restraint, but a copy of the doctor's prescription should stay in that vehicle at all times. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F14 | anchor: A01
Safety belts protect in five ways: they prevent ejection, shift crash forces onto the strongest bones, spread forces over a wide area, hold you in driving posture, and protect the head and spinal cord. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F15 | anchor: A01
Wear the lap belt low over the pelvis so its lower edge rests snugly on the tops of the thighs. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F16 | anchor: A01
The shoulder belt goes over the shoulder and across the chest, never under the arm or across the abdomen, and must not be so loose that it slips off. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F17 | anchor: A01
A pregnant woman should wear the lap belt below her abdomen and the shoulder belt above the belly. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec06-F18 | anchor: A02
A belted driver stays in the seat in a crash and is less likely to be knocked unconscious, so is better able to handle the emergency. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F19 | anchor: A02
The manual reports that proper lap and shoulder belt use cuts the risk of death for front-seat car occupants by 45 percent and of moderate-to-critical injury by 50 percent. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F20 | anchor: A02
According to the manual, not wearing a safety belt contributes to more traffic deaths than any other single safety behavior. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F21 | anchor: A02
The idea that belts trap you is a myth: a belt unbuckles in under a second, and crashes rarely end in fire or deep water. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F22 | anchor: A02
The manual says people thrown from a vehicle are four times as likely to be killed as those who stay inside it. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F23 | anchor: A02
In a side impact the car moves sideways and everything loose inside, passengers included, slides toward the point of impact, not away from it. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec06-F24 | anchor: A03
A child is big enough for the adult lap and shoulder belt once they can sit with their back against the seat back and their knees bend over the seat edge. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F25 | anchor: A03
On a child, the lap belt should sit low and snug on the upper thighs and the shoulder belt should cross the chest between neck and shoulder, never behind the back or under the arm. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F26 | anchor: A03
Under the belts-to-bones rule the pelvis and collarbone should take the belt's pressure, so if the belt rides on the stomach or crosses the face or neck, the child goes back to a booster seat. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F27 | anchor: A03
Air bags work best combined with safety belts, which together are the best protection available in a car, SUV or truck. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F28 | anchor: A03
Air bags are meant to keep occupants from striking the steering wheel or dashboard, and they inflate and deflate faster than a blink. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F29 | anchor: A03
Children aged 12 and under are safest in the back seat, properly restrained, whether or not the car has a passenger air bag. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F30 | anchor: A03
Do not put a child safety seat in the front seat of a car with a passenger air bag; place it in a rear seat if one exists. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F31 | anchor: A03
If a child must ride in front, as in a pickup truck with a passenger air bag, move the seat as far back as possible and buckle the child properly. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F32 | anchor: A03
Adults should always wear both lap and shoulder belts and sit far enough back to leave 10 to 12 inches between the chest and the air bag cover, as NHTSA recommends. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F33 | anchor: A03
Keep an adjustable steering wheel tilted down toward a level position. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F34 | anchor: A03
Tennessee forbids any child under 6 from riding in a pickup truck bed, and forbids children aged 6 to 12 from riding there on any state or interstate highway. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F35 | anchor: A03
A child may ride in a pickup bed during an organized parade or ceremony moving no faster than 20 mph, or during farm work. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F36 | anchor: A03
It is an offense to knowingly leave a child under 7 in a vehicle in a public place without supervision by someone at least 13 if conditions risk the child, the engine is running or the keys are inside. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F37 | anchor: A03
Leaving a young child unattended this way is a Class B misdemeanor fined $200 for a first offense and $500 for any later offense. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec06-F38 | anchor: A04
On a sunny summer day a car's interior can reach deadly heat within minutes, and harm can begin in as little as ten minutes. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec06-F39 | anchor: A04
Never leave a child alone in a vehicle, even for a quick errand, and check that everyone, including sleeping babies, is out when unloading. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec06-F40 | anchor: A04
If a child is locked inside a car, or you see a child or animal left alone in one, call 911. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0048]

Misconceptions: the front seat is not safer for a small child just because it has an air bag; a belt does not trap you in a crash; being thrown clear is far deadlier than staying inside; in a side crash you slide toward the impact, not away; a parent riding as a passenger is still responsible for the child's restraint.
Mnemonics: rear-facing under one or under twenty pounds; forward-facing one through three; booster four through eight under four foot nine; the back is where it's at for twelve and under; belts to bones.
Glossary: child restraint device means a car seat or booster seat; belt-positioning booster seat means a raised seat that makes the vehicle belt fit a child; ejection means being thrown out of the vehicle in a crash; air bag module means the cover on the wheel or dash that holds the air bag.
Dynamic facts: belt and child restraint fines, misdemeanor classes and the crash statistics the manual quotes can change; confirm them on official Tennessee sources before showing them to learners.
